issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is not very coherent for a captivity presentation as written: time-of-day could fit, but 'feeling happy or relaxed' and especially 'talks or photos about snakes' imply very different trigger themes without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking them to the captivity trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: Threat items mainly describe interpersonal pursuit/external danger (hypervigilance, checking if someone is following me, unsafe at night). That could fit captivity, but it is not well matched to the selected snake-related trigger or to body-monitoring for injury, producing a fragmented threat picture.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is much more severe and somewhat qualitatively different from the other negative appraisal items, which focus on helplessness and being unable to cope with trauma thoughts. It may occur in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' fits health/injury threat, but the threat items emphasize pursuit and ambush, while the triggers emphasize time-of-day, relaxation, and snakes. This coping strategy is therefore poorly linked to the rest of the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette:
Ajay, a 64-year-old warehouse worker, presented for therapy reporting a profound and unyielding sense of dread that had taken root eight months prior. The trauma occurred during a trip to his ancestral village in South Asia to celebrate a wedding. On his way back from a relative's home one evening, he was ambushed and taken captive, held for ransom for four days in a dark, earthen pit. His captors were a constant threat, but the most acute terror came on the second night when, in the faint moonlight, he saw a snake slithering over the dirt floor a few feet from where he lay. He remained frozen for hours, certain he would be bitten. Though the ransom was eventually paid and he was released physically unharmed, the experience fractured his belief in a predictable or safe world.

Upon returning to the US, Ajay tried to resume his life, but the terror had followed him home. He found that the fading light of dusk, the very time of day he was abducted, would trigger a cascade of fear. This initial trigger would instantly activate a profound sense of threat; he would begin to feel intensely unsafe, even in his own locked home, a feeling that only grew as night fell. He became hypervigilant, startled by the sound of a passing car or a floorboard creaking upstairs. Any mention or image of snakes, even in a nature documentary his wife was watching, would send a jolt of adrenaline through him, his heart pounding as if the reptile were in the room with him.

The nights quickly became unbearable. The darkness itself felt menacing, a direct reminder of the pit. This potent trigger led Ajay to develop strategies to keep the fear at bay. He began to actively avoid sleep, staying up with the lights blazing in the living room until he would collapse from exhaustion in the early hours of the morning. When he did sleep, he would often wake up in the pitch-black bedroom and feel a surge of panic, immediately starting to check his body for bites or injuries he was convinced he'd sustained. This constant body monitoring became a daytime ritual as well, a compulsive search for evidence of a danger he couldn't see.

Over the months, these behaviours have calcified into a devastating worldview. Ajay has come to believe that he is utterly helpless, that bad things are inevitable and he is powerless to stop them. This core appraisal that he cannot protect himself directly fuels his pervasive sense of threat; because he feels so vulnerable, he believes his only option is to remain constantly on guard. His attempts to manage this fear only reinforce his negative self-concept. He repeatedly asks his wife, "Are you sure the back door is locked?" or "Do you think I'm okay?" Seeking this reassurance provides a fleeting moment of relief, but each question deepens his conviction that he is a fragile, incapable man who is a burden to his family. The exhaustion from his sleep avoidance and the shame of his constant fear have led him to a dark conclusion: he is not sure his life is worth living anymore.

The strategies Ajay uses to survive have, in a cruel irony, made his world even more dangerous. His chronic sleep deprivation leaves his nerves raw, making him more susceptible to his triggers. By staying awake to fend off the darkness, he immerses himself for hours in the very nighttime environment he fears, amplifying its power over him. His life has now shrunk. The walk from the warehouse doors to his car after his evening shift has become a nightly ordeal. He finds himself constantly looking over his shoulder, certain he is being followed, his keys clutched in his hand like a weapon. The hypervigilance has become so ingrained that he feels hunted even in the most familiar of spaces.

Ajay finally agreed to seek help after his wife found him at the kitchen table at dawn, staring blankly at the wall, having not slept for two nights straight. He confessed to her his deepest fear, one he had been holding in for months: he was convinced that if he ever truly allowed himself to think about what happened in that pit, the memory would shatter what was left of his mind. He came to his first session not with any real hope, but with a quiet desperation, asking if it was possible for a man his age to ever feel safe in his own home after the sun went down.
